concepts.description: An algorithm design strategy that splits a problem into smaller independent subproblems, solves them recursively, and combines their results. Merge sort and quicksort are presented as its main examples.
concepts.name: Divide-and-Conquer

concepts.description: A method for solving recurrence relations of the form T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n) to obtain asymptotic bounds. It is used to analyze the running time of divide-and-conquer algorithms.
concepts.name: Master Theorem

concepts.description: A technique where a function solves a problem by calling itself on smaller subproblems until reaching a base case. In this lecture it serves as the foundation for divide-and-conquer methods.
concepts.name: Recursion

concepts.description: A divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm that recursively splits an array in half, sorts each half, and merges the sorted halves in linear time, giving O(n log n) worst-case performance.
concepts.name: Merge Sort

concepts.description: A divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm that partitions an array around a pivot element and recursively sorts the partitions. It is typically fast in practice but its worst case depends on pivot choice.
concepts.name: Quicksort

concepts.description: A top-down optimization technique that caches the results of recursive calls so each subproblem is computed only once. It converts exponential recursive solutions into polynomial-time ones.
concepts.name: Memoization

concepts.description: An approach that fills a table of subproblem solutions iteratively, starting from the smallest subproblems, to avoid recursion overhead. It is the iterative counterpart of memoization.
concepts.name: Bottom-Up Dynamic Programming

concepts.description: Algorithms that make locally optimal choices at each step, aiming for a globally optimal solution. The lecture discusses when this strategy provably works.
concepts.name: Greedy Algorithms

concepts.description: An abstract combinatorial structure that characterizes when a greedy algorithm yields an optimal solution. It formalizes independence systems in which greedy selection is guaranteed to succeed.
concepts.name: Matroid Framework

concepts.description: A classic dynamic programming problem that finds the longest sequence appearing in the same relative order in two strings. It is a standard example of the DP table technique.
concepts.name: Longest Common Subsequence

concepts.description: A classic dynamic programming problem that selects items with given weights and values to maximize total value under a capacity constraint. It illustrates DP over choices and capacities.
concepts.name: Knapsack Problem

concepts.description: A classic dynamic programming problem that computes the minimum number of insertions, deletions, and substitutions needed to transform one string into another.
concepts.name: Edit Distance
